evidence.claim: A mountainside road shortened the journey between Newburgh and West Point.
evidence.quote: When it was opened in 1922 it shortened the distance required to travel by automobile from Newburgh to West Point

evidence.claim: Storm King Highway winds along the steep slopes above the Hudson, reaching 420 feet above the water.
evidence.quote: It is so named because it winds around the steep slopes of Storm King Mountain near its north end of the Hudson Highlands on the west bank of the Hudson River. Here it reaches heights of up to 420 feet (130 m) above the water

evidence.claim: This two-lane section of NY 218 has a rubblestone wall on its river side and grades no steeper than 7 percent.
evidence.quote: Storm King Highway is a two-lane 22-foot-wide (6.7 m) asphalt-paved road with double yellow lines forbidding passing along its entire 21,000-foot (6,400 m) length. Its grade never exceeds 7%, and it is bounded along the river side with a rubblestone wall.

evidence.claim: Its civil engineering earned National Register recognition in 1982.
evidence.quote: added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1982 in recognition of its accomplishment in civil engineering.

evidence.claim: Local business and community groups pressed for a connection through the Highlands; highway commissioner Gordon Reel took up the idea in 1913.
evidence.quote: In 1913 state highway commissioner Gordon Reel began to think seriously about building a new road to connect them after heavy lobbying by local business and community groups.

evidence.claim: Surveyors sometimes rappelled down cliffs to mark the route before construction began in 1916.
evidence.quote: After three years, during which surveyors sometimes had to rappel down the mountain's cliffs to mark the route, construction began in 1916.

evidence.claim: A proposed tunnel gave way to an open cut because lighting would cost too much and the tunnel would miss the scenery.
evidence.quote: The original idea to build a tunnel was changed to a road cut into the side as lighting it would have been too expensive and it would have missed the most scenic aspects of the road.

evidence.claim: The 1922 opening cut 22 miles from the automobile journey between Newburgh and West Point.
evidence.quote: When it was opened in 1922 it shortened the distance required to travel by automobile from Newburgh to West Point, which are 10 miles (16 km) apart as the crow flies, by 22 miles (34 km).

evidence.claim: Traveling south from Cornwall-on-Hudson, the historic section runs to Lee Road in the Town of Highlands.
evidence.quote: between Lee Road in the Town of Highlands at the south end and the Cornwall-on-Hudson village line

evidence.claim: Small pullouts offer views of the Hudson and mountains including Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill.
evidence.quote:
with panoramic views of the river and surrounding mountains such as Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill.
Several small pullouts allow drivers to stop and enjoy the view.

evidence.claim: Highland Falls lies beside the United States Military Academy at West Point.
evidence.quote: Highland Falls is in the Town of Highlands and is adjacent to the United States Military Academy at West Point.

evidence.claim: Camp Olmsted occupies land on Bayview Avenue, NY 218, near Storm King Mountain.
evidence.quote: It is located along Bayview Avenue, NY 218, near Storm King Mountain.

evidence.claim: The Methodist Five Points Mission founded the camp in 1901 for children of immigrant families it helped in Manhattan.
evidence.quote: Camp Olmsted is a summer camp and retreat in Cornwall-on-Hudson, New York, operated by the Five Points Mission, a Methodist organization.

evidence.claim: The camp began with a parcel of 21 acres donated by Sarah and John Olmsted, under the name Olmsted Fresh Air Home.
evidence.quote: Sarah and John Olmsted donated the 21-acre (8 ha) parcel that was originally known as the Olmsted Fresh Air Home.

evidence.claim: Campers traveled from the city to Cornwall aboard the Hudson River Day Liner.
evidence.quote: Campers would take the Hudson River Day Liner from the city to Cornwall and then proceed to the camp.

evidence.claim: Winterizing three cabins allowed year-round operation in 1966; the camp continues to serve city children in summer and host religious retreats throughout the year.
evidence.quote: In 1966 the New York City Society took a role in operating the camp, which, when three cabins were winterized, allowed for year-round operation.

evidence.claim: The Methodist Five Points Mission founded the camp in 1901 for children of immigrant families it helped in Manhattan.
evidence.quote: It was founded in 1901 when the mission, which had been working to improve conditions for residents of the eponymous Manhattan slum (depicted in the Martin Scorsese film Gangs of New York) since 1848. At the turn of the century, they realized children from the immigrant families they were helping needed a place to get away from the city during the summer.

evidence.claim: the camp continues to serve city children in summer and host religious retreats throughout the year.
evidence.quote: Today the camp runs four 12-day sessions for city children in the summer, and religious retreats year-round.

evidence.claim: The pullouts give views across the Hudson toward Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill.
evidence.quote:
with panoramic views of the river and surrounding mountains such as Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill.
Several small pullouts allow drivers to stop and enjoy the view.

evidence.claim: Building this road meant working above another transport route: the New York Central Railroad’s West Shore Line.
evidence.quote: the New York Central Railroad's West Shore Line, which ran along the river's edge below.

evidence.claim: Dislodged boulders sometimes blocked its tracks or damaged rail cars and their contents.
evidence.quote: Dislodged boulders sometimes blocked the tracks or landed on cars, damaging them and their contents.

evidence.claim: The mountain remains a source of hazards, including rockfall and falling ice.
evidence.quote: Due to hazards of rockfall as well as avalanches and falling ice

evidence.claim: In July 2023, a flash flood washed out both lanes and the retaining wall along an entire section of highway.
evidence.quote: Following a flash flood in July 2023, an entire section of the highway, including both lanes and the retaining wall, was washed out.

evidence.claim: The Department of Transportation closes the road during heavy rain or snow because of rockfall, avalanche and falling-ice hazards.
evidence.quote: Due to hazards of rockfall as well as avalanches and falling ice, the road is closed by the state Department of Transportation during periods of heavy rain or snow.

evidence.claim: Round brick arches frame the upper windows of Highland Falls Village Hall, a three-story brick building on Main Street.
evidence.quote: The windows on the second and third stories are framed by projecting round brick arches

evidence.claim: The local tax assessor dates the building to 1894, though its exact construction year and original purpose are unknown.
evidence.quote: The exact year of the building's construction, and its original purpose, is not known. A brick building is shown at the site on maps from 1859 and 1875, but not 1891. The local tax assessor dates the building to 1894.

evidence.claim: First National Bank acquired it in 1907, when storefronts were added and the southernmost upper windows were bricked in.
evidence.quote: In 1907, records show that a Mr. Kreutz sold the building to the First National Bank of Highland Falls. At that time alterations were made to the exterior. Storefronts were added and the southernmost upper windows bricked in.

evidence.claim: The village bought the property in 1967 and has used it without significant alterations since.
evidence.quote: In 1967 the village acquired the property. It has used it ever since, without any significant alterations.

evidence.claim: a three-story brick building on Main Street.
evidence.quote: The Highland Falls Village Hall is located on Main Street in Highland Falls, New York, United States. It is a three-story Italianate-style brick buildings

evidence.claim: The first contractor went bankrupt, and its replacement faced a labor shortage when the United States entered World War I. The Palisades Interstate Park Commission renegotiated the contract to account for those wartime difficulties.
evidence.quote: The first contractor hired for the job soon went bankrupt; they were replaced by the John L. Hayes Company of Yonkers. Hayes, too, found the going tough, especially when U.S. entry into World War I dried up the labor supply. The PIPC soon stepped in and renegotiated the contract to account for the difficulties caused to Hayes by the unforeseen circumstance of war.

evidence.claim: In 1940, four-lane US 9W west of Storm King shortened the journey further.
evidence.quote: In 1940 this distance was further cut by the four-lane U.S. Route 9W, which travels west of Storm King.

evidence.claim: A rubblestone wall borders the river side of the road, and chainlink gates stand at both ends.
evidence.quote: Its grade never exceeds 7%, and it is bounded along the river side with a rubblestone wall.

evidence.claim: chainlink gates stand at both ends.
evidence.quote: There are chainlink gates at either end.

evidence.claim: Glass storefronts remain at street level, north of the central entrance with its round arch and fluted pilasters.
evidence.quote: There are glass storefronts at street level north of the centrally located main entrance, round-arched and supported by fluted pilasters.

evidence.claim: A rubblestone wall follows the river side of the highway.
evidence.quote: it is bounded along the river side with a rubblestone wall.
